opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few things going on at once.

The first is simply contamination. For most of the history of NLP, you could build a test set, put it out there, and reasonably assume that the models people were evaluating hadn't seen it. That assumption is basically gone now. These models are trained on enormous swaths of the web, and any benchmark that's been public for a while has almost certainly leaked into the training data in some form, whether that's the actual items, discussions of them, or close paraphrases. So you're never quite sure whether you're measuring capability or memorization.

The second is that the models have gotten good enough that the easy-to-construct benchmarks saturate very quickly. It used to be that a dataset like SQuAD or GLUE would have a useful life of several years. Now you put out something hard and within months the top systems are near ceiling. To stay ahead, you need questions that are genuinely difficult, and making difficult questions with unambiguous, verifiable answers is expensive. You need domain experts, and you need careful vetting, because at the high end a surprising fraction of benchmark errors are actually errors in the gold labels.

Third, and this is the deeper issue, especially for something like world models, a lot of what we actually care about doesn't decompose nicely into multiple-choice questions or short answers. We want to know: does the system have a coherent model of how things work? Can it reason about consequences, handle novel situations, maintain consistency over a long interaction, plan? Those are properties of extended behavior, and they're much harder to score automatically. Once you go to open-ended generation, you're back to the old problem of evaluation, and the field has increasingly been using models as judges, which is useful but introduces its own biases and circularity.

And then finally there's Goodhart's law. As soon as a benchmark becomes the thing that leaderboards and press releases are built around, people optimize for it, sometimes quite indirectly, through choices about training data and post-training. The benchmark stops being a neutral measurement and becomes a target.

So I think the way forward is some combination of things: held-out and regularly refreshed test sets, more evaluation in realistic interactive settings rather than static question answering, and being a bit more humble about what any single number tells you. In some ways, linguistics and cognitive science have long known that measuring understanding is hard. We're just now running into that with machines in a very concrete way.

r001.rationale: The response says important capabilities such as reasoning about consequences, handling novel situations, consistency over long interactions, and planning do not fit neatly into multiple-choice or short-answer tasks, making them harder to evaluate.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think there are a few things going on, and they compound each other.

The first is just that the models got good. For a long time, the way benchmarks worked in NLP was that you'd pick some task that humans could do and machines couldn't, you'd build a dataset, and you'd watch the numbers climb for five or six years. Parsing, question answering, natural language inference. And that worked because there was a long runway. Now the runway is six months, sometimes less. You release something, it's saturated before the paper is even reviewed, and then you're left arguing about whether the last few points of headroom are signal or label noise. So the half-life of a benchmark has collapsed, and that's demoralizing for the people who build them, because building a good one is a lot of work.

The second problem is contamination, and I don't just mean the obvious case where the test set ends up in the pretraining data, though that happens constantly. The subtler thing is that once you train on the whole internet, almost any task you can write down has something close to it out there already. So you're never quite measuring generalization in the way you thought you were. You're measuring some mixture of reasoning and recall, and nobody can tell you the ratio.

And then the third thing, which I think is actually the deepest, is that we've lost agreement about what we're trying to measure. With world models in particular, the question is something like, does this system have a coherent internal representation of how the world works? Does it know that if you put a cup on a table and tilt the table, the cup slides? But you can only probe that through behavior, through text or through some simulated environment. And a model can get the right answer for the wrong reason, or get the wrong answer because of some artifact of the prompt. The thing you care about is latent, and the thing you can score is surface. That gap was always there, but when models were weak it didn't matter much, because they failed in ways that were obviously about understanding. Now they fail in ways that are strange and hard to attribute.

I'd add that there's an incentive problem too. Benchmarks are now part of marketing. Every lab wants to report a number, and every number gets optimized. So the moment something becomes a standard, it stops being a good measurement, which is basically Goodhart's law operating at industrial scale.

So where does that leave us? I think the useful work now is in things that are harder to game: held-out private evaluations, dynamic benchmarks that get regenerated, long-horizon tasks where you actually have to maintain state over many steps. And honestly, careful qualitative analysis, which the field has sometimes looked down on. Reading a few hundred outputs with a skeptical eye tells you things a leaderboard never will. It's less satisfying than a single number going up, but I think we're going to have to get comfortable with that.

r001.rationale: The response discusses benchmark saturation, contamination, and the difficulty of measuring latent world understanding through observable behavior, but it does not clearly attribute the difficulty to a mismatch between conventional question-answering tasks and what users increasingly want models to do.

astra-6.text:
I think the central difficulty is that we want to measure something much broader than success on a particular task. With a world model, we’d like to know whether a system understands how things work well enough to predict what will happen in a new situation. But all we observe is its answers, and it’s surprisingly difficult to tell whether those answers reflect that understanding or some regularity it has picked up in the data.

That’s particularly acute for text models, because language contains an enormous amount of information about the world. A model can give a very convincing explanation of a physical situation. Does that mean it can reason about what happens when you change the situation? Sometimes yes, sometimes no. A benchmark needs to distinguish those cases, rather than just reward a familiar-looking answer.

And then there’s the practical problem of scale. When models have been trained on so much text, it becomes difficult to establish that your test is genuinely new. Even if the exact questions weren’t in the training data, very similar problems may have been. Once a benchmark becomes popular, people also optimize for it, and it gradually becomes less useful as an independent measure.

So I think we need more evaluation where you can vary the conditions, ask follow-up questions, and test whether a model’s predictions remain consistent. But designing that well is much harder than assembling a set of questions with an answer key.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmarks should measure broad understanding and distinguish reasoning from familiar patterns, but it does not clearly attribute the difficulty to a mismatch between conventional question-answering tasks and what users increasingly want models to do.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think part of the problem is that we’ve become very good at solving the benchmarks that we know how to construct. If you can turn something into a large collection of relatively short questions with clear answers, that’s exactly the kind of thing these models can learn to do well. But that doesn’t necessarily tell you whether they have a robust understanding of the world, or whether they can use that understanding in a new situation.

And then there’s the issue that the benchmarks themselves become part of the ecosystem. People train on related material, they optimize against the results, and sometimes the actual test examples end up in training data. So it becomes difficult to disentangle generalization from familiarity.

For world models, there’s an additional difficulty: what do you mean by having a good model of the world? Predicting what someone will say about an event is one thing. Predicting what will happen if you intervene—if you move an object or change a condition—is a stronger requirement. You’d like to test that across unfamiliar situations, and over multiple steps, where errors have consequences.

So I think the challenge is to move toward evaluating the ability to do things in varied environments, while still having enough control that you can say what a result means. It’s much easier to produce a single benchmark score than to establish that kind of competence.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts short, clear-answer questions with the desired abilities to handle unfamiliar situations, predict intervention outcomes, and perform across varied environments, conveying the mismatch between conventional QA benchmarks and broader model capabilities.
